patient.chief_complaint: Bilateral foot numbness and tingling, worse at night, for 2.5 years
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Johnson is a 58-year-old African American woman with an 11-year history of type 2 diabetes who presents for evaluation of bilateral foot numbness and tingling that has been progressively worsening over the past 2.5 years. She describes the sensation as a constant tingling, like pins and needles, predominantly in her toes and the balls of her feet. More recently, she has developed a burning quality to the pain that is particularly bothersome at night, disrupting her sleep 3 to 4 times per week. The numbness has gradually extended from her toes to involve both feet entirely, and she now notes some numbness in the lower 6 inches of both legs. She reports difficulty feeling the texture of the ground while walking and has noted she cannot feel water temperature with her feet. Last month, she stepped on a small piece of glass and did not feel it until her daughter noticed blood on the floor. She has had recurrent small cuts and calluses on her feet that she only notices when bathing. She acknowledges her blood sugars have been inconsistently controlled, with home readings ranging widely from 80 to over 300 mg/dL. She has been compliant with her insulin and oral medications but admits dietary challenges. She denies upper extremity symptoms, weakness, or difficulty walking. She denies recent illness, new medications, or toxic exposures. Her hypothyroidism was diagnosed 4 years ago and she states her last TSH was within normal range per her primary care physician.

findings.nerve: EMG - right first dorsal interosseous foot

specialized_test.impression: Moderately severe length-dependent axonal sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy. Sural SNAPs are absent or markedly reduced bilaterally; superficial peroneal sensory is absent on the right. Lower extremity motor amplitudes are reduced with prolonged F-wave latency; upper extremity median and motor studies are preserved. No demyelinating features — no temporal dispersion, no conduction block, conduction velocities proportional to axonal loss. EMG demonstrates chronic denervation distally. Findings are consistent with a moderate-to-severe length-dependent axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy

quantitative_data.pattern: Distal sudomotor and cardiovagal autonomic neuropathy

output.impression: Moderate distal autonomic dysfunction — QSART absent at foot and markedly reduced at distal leg (0.15 uL/cm2; reference >0.3); cardiovagal studies show reduced heart rate variability (E:I ratio 1.06; Valsalva ratio 1.15, both below normal thresholds). Mild orthostatic hypotension confirmed on orthostatic testing (BP drop 18/8 mmHg at 2 min, symptomatic). Findings are consistent with predominantly distal sudomotor and cardiovagal autonomic neuropathy

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is a cortical test and is non-contributory in peripheral nerve disease.
Head/brain CT has no role in peripheral neuropathy evaluation.
Brain MRI is not indicated in typical distal symmetric polyneuropathy without CNS signs.
Advanced cerebral imaging (PET/MRA/MRV/perfusion) has no routine role in peripheral neuropathy.
Echocardiography is not indicated unless cardiac amyloid is suspected.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated unless there is syncope or symptomatic dysautonomia with arrhythmia concern.

sequence_constraints.reason: Tier the workup — basic labs first, then targeted electrodiagnostic and tissue studies.

critical_actions: Address both diabetic and B12 contributors
B12 supplementation (parenteral if severe; oral 1000 mcg daily otherwise)
contraindicated_actions: Do not give folate alone if B12 deficient — risk of worsening neurologic damage
key_reasoning_points: Multifactorial neuropathy: diabetes + B12 deficiency; both must be treated
Reversible factors (B12) can plateau or partially reverse with replacement
